name: Time Dilation
what: This subtopic covers the concept of proper time, dilated time, and the Lorentz factor. Students learn to identify which observer measures proper time and apply the equation t = γt₀ to calculate time intervals in different reference frames.
why: Time dilation is one of the most experimentally verified predictions of special relativity, confirmed by atomic clocks on aircraft and by the observed lifetimes of fast-moving particles. It underpins GPS corrections and particle physics calculations.

items.title: I can define proper time (t₀) and identify which observer measures it
items.what: Proper time is the time interval between two events measured in the reference frame where both events occur at the same point in space. It is always the shortest time interval measured for those two events.
items.why: Correctly identifying who measures proper time is the critical first step in applying the time dilation formula. Applying the formula backwards gives an incorrect, physically impossible answer.
items.example: A clock on a rocket ticks twice. The rocket crew sees both ticks happen at the same location (the clock), so they measure proper time. An Earth observer sees the clock move between the two ticks, so they measure dilated time.

items.title: I can define dilated time (t) and explain why it is longer than proper time
items.what: Dilated time is the time interval between two events measured by an observer in a frame where the two events occur at different points in space. It is always longer than the proper time for the same pair of events.
items.why: Because the speed of light is constant, an observer who sees the light clock move must observe the light travel a longer diagonal path — meaning more time must pass in their frame.
items.example: A rocket crew measures a light flash lasting 0.100 s (proper time). An Earth observer watching the rocket pass at 0.866c measures the same flash lasting 0.200 s — the dilated time.

items.title: I can define and calculate the Lorentz factor (γ)
items.what: The Lorentz factor γ = 1 / √(1 − v²/c²) describes how much time, length, and energy differ between two reference frames. It is always greater than or equal to 1, and increases toward infinity as v approaches c.
items.why: The Lorentz factor appears in every relativistic equation. Being able to calculate it quickly and accurately is essential for all time dilation, length contraction, and energy calculations.

items.title: I can apply the time dilation formula t = γt₀ to find dilated time or proper time
items.what: The equation t = γt₀ relates proper time t₀ (measured by the observer for whom the events occur at the same place) to dilated time t (measured by any other observer). Since γ ≥ 1, dilated time is always greater than or equal to proper time.
items.why: This formula is the primary mathematical tool for time dilation problems in VCE Physics. It is applied in contexts ranging from particle decay to GPS satellite corrections.
items.example: A muon at rest decays after t₀ = 2.20 × 10⁻⁶ s. Moving at 0.995c (γ = 10.01), an Earth observer measures t = 10.01 × 2.20 × 10⁻⁶ = 2.20 × 10⁻⁵ s.

items.title: I can calculate the speed of an object given proper time and dilated time measurements
items.what: By rearranging t = γt₀ to find γ, and then rearranging γ = 1 / √(1 − v²/c²) to find v, it is possible to determine the relative speed between two frames from time measurements alone.
items.why: This reverse calculation is a common exam question style. It tests deep understanding of the relationship between γ and velocity, not just formula recall.
items.example: A particle is observed to decay after 45.2 ps when moving and 3.44 ps when at rest. γ = 45.2 / 3.44 = 13.14. Then v/c = √(1 − 1/13.14²) = 0.997, so v = 0.997c.

items.title: I can explain what happens to dilated time as relative speed increases
items.what: As relative speed increases, the Lorentz factor γ increases. This means the difference between proper time and dilated time grows larger. As v approaches c, dilated time approaches infinity.
items.why: Understanding this trend qualitatively allows students to check whether calculated answers are physically reasonable and to explain graph-based questions about relativistic effects.
items.example: At v = 0.5c, γ ≈ 1.15, so a 1-second proper time becomes 1.15 s dilated. At v = 0.99c, γ ≈ 7.09, so the same 1-second proper time becomes 7.09 s dilated.
